newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Mandela says situation in Swaziland explosive.
newsitem.headline: Mandela says situation in Swaziland explosive.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela said on Thursday that the situation in Swaziland, where strikers are trying to bring down an absolute monarchy, was "explosive".
A national strike began 10 days ago in the small southern African state, where trade unions seeking democratic change have crippled the country's vital sugar and timber export industries.
"We would want to see the situation in Swaziland unfold to democracy as the king has promised us but our situation is to facilitate not to intervene," Mandela said on a brief visit to Zimbabwe.
Police have fired on strikers, wounding several people, and the government headed by King Mswati III has arrested three trade union leaders.
Mandela told Zimbabwe state television on arrival for a whistle-stop meeting with Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe that the situation in the mountain kingdom was explosive.

Mugabe said southern African states would "not intervene but (rather) try to encourage" a resolution of the political problems in Swaziland and in Lesotho, another mountain kingdom in southern Africa with political tensions.
Last Thursday mutinous policemen seized control of police headquarters in Lesotho and called for a national police strike.

"We are all worried in the region about the development in Swaziland and Lesotho but our role will not be in intervention, but to try to encourage them and persuade them and support them to establish democracy," Mugabe said.
Mugabe was briefing reporters about his three-hour meeting with Mandela which covered several African problems, including the Angolan peace process and the Zaire civil war.

But the Zimbabwean president -- who is also chairman of the Southern African Development Community (SADC) organ on politics, defence and security -- gave no details on Zaire and the Great Lakes region, where he said SADC would support peace efforts by countries in that region.
SADC is made up of Angola, Botswana, Malawi, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, Lesotho, South Africa, Swaziland, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe.

Mandela, who left Harare for Botswana for similar talks with President Sir Ketumile Masire, said he had spoken to United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Wednesday night on some African conflicts.
Mandela said collective efforts were necessary to solve the conflicts, including in Angola where the peace process has stalled over the status of UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi.
Mugabe said it was necessary for the veteran Angolan guerrilla leader to contribute effectively in establishing lasting peace.
"We must try and get Savimbi to participate effectively in the peace process so that he becomes a part of the peaceful solution," he said.
